title: The trees that saw him off
hookLine: the trees on Mahendra fly after Hanuman like family seeing off a traveler; why Hindu families walk you out and bless you
carry: ashirvad: a blessing goes where family can't

lines: AS FAR AS THEY CAN GO.
cards: Valmiki gives Hanuman's leap an escort. The force of his takeoff tears the flowering trees on Mahendra loose, and they fly up after him.
It's a picture from ordinary life, borrowed for a mountain: the parent at the school gate, the one who comes as far as they can and then has to stop.
Hanuman is about to cross a hundred yojanas alone, and the trees go with him as far as trees can.

teach.b: Valmiki makes the comparison himself: the trees follow Hanuman for a while like relatives seeing off someone dear, and then, one by one, they drop into the ocean, and their blossoms float on the dark water like stars.
Then he turns to Hanuman: arms outstretched, eyes shining, his shadow moving over the waves like a ship under sail.
And the gods, the celestial singers and the great sages watch from the sky and shower him with flowers and praise. Valmiki didn't need to explain the picture of relatives turning back.
His listeners knew it, and the epic shows it elsewhere: when Rama leaves for exile, the people of Ayodhya follow his chariot until they can't. It's a Hindu courtesy still kept.
You walk them to the door, the gate, the car, and you send them with a blessing. That blessing has a name: ashirvad.
Before a journey, an exam or a wedding, many Hindus touch an elder's feet, and the elder's hand comes down on their head. Some families add a spoonful of curd and sugar for a good start.

teach.h: ASHIRVAD: A BLESSING GOES WHERE FAMILY CAN'T.
teach.b: The idea under it, as many families put it: a blessing goes where the family can't. And Hanuman himself lived it.
Before he leapt, Valmiki says, he folded his hands and bowed to the Sun, to Indra, to Brahma, and to his father the Wind. The trees fell. The flowers from the sky kept coming.
Hanuman crosses alone, but he doesn't cross unblessed.

how: Many Hindu families still walk a departing guest or traveler out, and before journeys and exams children touch elders' feet for ashirvad; devotional paintings often show Hanuman in midair over the sea with flowers falling around him.

o: Hanuman's jump back home from Lanka with news
the trees' flight after him from Mahendra
Hanuman's flight across the sea toward Lanka

p: follow him like family seeing him off
like stars on the dark sea
an elder's blessing before you set out

s: the trees torn up by his takeoff fly after him for a while
then they fall into the sea, like relatives turning back.
other monkeys fly with Hanuman to Lanka
many Hindus ask an elder's blessing before journeys, exams, a new job: anything that starts something.

games.q: your cousin leaves for college tomorrow. by today's story, what does a Hindu family do?
o: say bye from the couch; she's an adult now.
walk her out and give her a blessing for the road.
go with her the whole way so she's never alone.
games.why: like the trees, the family goes as far as it can, then sends ashirvad, a blessing, the rest of the way.

practice: Bring to mind one person setting out on something this week: a trip, a test, a hard day. If you pray, fold your hands and ask a blessing for them, in whatever words your family uses.
If you don't, picture walking them to the door, as far as you can go, and sending something good with them the rest of the way. Breathe in, walking with them. Breathe out, letting them go on.

wordCard.voice: The leap. Hanuman's crossing, with trees falling behind him like family seeing off a traveler, and his shadow sailing below him like a ship.

orig.note: Sanskrit āśīrvāda, a blessing, especially an elder's, spoken over someone setting out.

carryVoice: Your line: ashirvad, a blessing goes where family can't. Out over the sea, someone is about to offer him a rest. See you tomorrow.
